titleStmt.title: Memorandum From the President’s Assistant for National Security Affairs (Clark) to President Reagan

div.head: 376. Memorandum From the President’s Assistant for National Security Affairs (Clark) to President Reagan
div.p: Our main objective should be to buttress President Hurtado’s effort to maintain democracy in Ecuador. Our political support has helped him in this regard. By demonstrating our strong commitment to the democratic system, we will give a clear message not only to Hurtado’s allies but to his adversaries as well and to the hemisphere generally. President Hurtado probably will seek additional U.S. assistance in overcoming Ecuador’s current economic crisis. He may also comment generally on the hemisphere’s debt problems. Ecuador is also seeking reconsideration of the recent increase in Panama Canal tolls.

Hurtado assumed the Presidency in 1981 when President Roldos was killed in an aircraft accident. Hurtado has managed his portfolio as well as could be expected given Ecuador’s fledgling democracy, unstable economy, and erratic foreign policy. Economic activity, aggravated by a failure to adjust spending patterns to lower petroleum prices, is the lowest it has been in years. This has resulted in discontent in the business and labor communities and within the military. Inflation is 30 percent. The business community distrusts President Hurtado’s motives; and the military has been plotting to unseat him almost since he assumed power. Hurtado’s decision to impose austerity measures needed for a $170M stand-by agreement with the IMF prompted a potentially dangerous general strike last month. Despite political unrest and severe economic problems, Ecuador does not have a guerrilla or terrorist problem.

Because of the many problems he faces across a broad spectrum, Hurtado’s primary goal is to see Ecuador through to next year’s elections. Relations between our countries are generally excellent. We have recently lifted our tuna embargo and should indicate support for Hurtado’s economic reform measures and efforts to reach agreement with the IMF.
[Omitted here are a list of participants, a press plan, and a schedule.]

note.p: Source: Reagan Library, Executive Secretariat, NSC Country File, Latin America/Central, Ecuador (03/29/1983–11/01/1983). Top Secret. Prepared by North. Copies were sent to Bush, Meese, Baker, and Deaver. Reagan signed his initials at the top of the page. No memoranda of conversation have been found. Attached as Tab A, but not printed, are talking points. Attached as Tab B, but not printed, is Shultz’s March 31 memorandum to Reagan. See Document 375. Attached as Tab C, but not printed, are background papers, papers on the political situation, the economic situation, foreign relations, and the Panama Canal tolls, and a CIA Special Analysis/Bio Brief. Tab D, a departure statement, was not attached. Reagan and Hurtado’s remarks are in Public Papers: Reagan, 1983, Book I, p. 517. Hurtado visited Washington for an official working visit April 7–9. According to the President’s Daily Diary, on April 8 Hurtado met with Reagan in the Oval Office from 11:36 a.m to 12:17 p.m, followed by a working luncheon in the State Dining Room from 12:17 to 1:25 p.m. (Reagan Library, President’s Daily Diary)

Reagan wrote in his personal diary on April 8: “Pres. Hurtado of Ecuador arrived—a good meeting & working lunch in the St. Dining Room. He’s an intelligent young man and dedicated to maintaining the new found democracy in his country & wants to see it spread throughout Central & So. America.” (Brinkley, ed., The Reagan Diaries, vol. I, January 1981–October 1985, p. 214)

See footnote 5, Document 375. In telegram 3004 from Quito, April 18, the Embassy wrote: “Several April 17 newspapers carried an Ecuadorean Foreign Ministry statement denying the signing of a fishing agreement with the United States recently. The denial was prompted by the allusion made by an Ecuadorean TV panelist April 14 to President Reagan’s White House remarks April 8 in the presence of President Hurtado. The panelist, ex-Foreign Minister and opposition alternate Congressman (CID) Julio Prado, chose to construe the White House remarks as suggesting a behind-the-scenes quid pro quo for lifting of the Ecuador tuna embargo.” The Embassy added that the Ecuadorean “clarification highlighted Ecuador’s claim to jurisdiction over tuna within the 200-mile zone.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D830215–0908)
